newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech floods could swamp impact of crown float.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech floods could swamp impact of crown float.

text.p: Two months after the Czech crown was floated and the government ordered austerity measures to restore economic balance, analysts say the impact is evident but recent severe floods could sweep things off course.

The yawning trade and current account deficits which helped spark speculative selling ahead of the flotation on May 27 remain the key economic problems. Analysts say that costly relief efforts after floods devastated parts of the eastern Czech Republic will make bridging the gaps all the harder.

"The flooding will change many things. It will increase the need for financing from the state budget quite dramatically and now nobody expects reaching complete balance in the state budget at the end of the year," said Zivnostenska Banka chief economist Pavel Sobisek.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) decision to float the crown followed weeks of turmoil on the foreign exchange markets. Investors had dumped the currency on worries of a current account deficit of around nine percent of gross domestic product and a widening, consumption-fuelled trade gap.
Political uncertainty over the fate of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's government, now less acute, added to the concern.

After the float, the crown immediately weakened to 11 percent below the midpoint of its old dollar/mark basket. It has since come back to about 10 percent below parity as interest rates, raised sharply to protect it, have gradually been lowered.
WEAKER CROWN MAY HELP EXPORTS
The day after the float, Klaus announced his second austerity package in as many months.

It included a freeze on public sector wages and budget cuts to balance the 1997 budget, a "slightly" surplus 1998 budget, import restrictions and support for CNB policies to cut inflation and stabilise the crown. The government survived a parliamentary confidence motion by one vote on June 10.

Some politicians questioned if currency exchange restrictions might be re-imposed. The central bank did limit foreign access to the money market during the height of the crisis, but the government's commitment to a fully exchangeable crown remains undiminished.
In announcing the austerity package, Czech coalition leaders acknowledged the crisis was a sign of the depth of the country's problems but also of the economy's openness.

"The currency crisis of the last days, despite having its speculative component which the Czech economy faces for the first time ever, showed the linkage of our economy to the world, the fragility and vulnerability of new economic relations, and the depth of our economic and above all balance of payment problems," the leaders said in a joint statement.

Since the float, trade data have been improving. June figures, published last week, showed the deficit narrowed to 9.6 billion crowns ($278.5 million) from 11 billion in May and 13.6 billion in June 1996. Exports rose 31 percent in June 1997.
"I would attribute 80 percent of the improvement to the weaker crown and the remainder to the government's demand management measures," said WoodCommerz economist Jiri Krovak.
There have also been signs of a slowdown in booming wage growth, which has been stoking demand for imports.
June data, published this week, showed average industrial wages grew 16.0 percent in nominal terms after 11.9 percent in May and 13.3 percent in June 1996.
But in the first six months of 1997, wages rose 13.8 percent year-on-year, compared with 17.5 percent in the whole of 1996.
"There is some improvement and this has come before all the steps taken by the government," said Patria Finance economist Vladimir Kreidl.
He said the public sector wage freeze would only have an indirect impact on industrial wages and that it would be apparent only later in the year.
FLOODS CHANGE THE PICTURE

Economists have put the cost of the damage at 50-100 billion crowns. Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said last week the floods would cut tax revenues by 10 billion crowns this year but the 1998 budget would be drawn up in balance.
Zivnostenska Banka's Sobisek said he believed the state budget deficit could hit 20 billion crowns this year and that, with other public sector budgets, it could be two percent of GDP.
"This is negative but it is quite possible that this expectation has already been reflected in the exchange rate of the crown," he added.
"It is still possible that the depreciation (of the crown) will turn out to be sufficient to reach a macroeconomic balance in the second half of 1997."

He saw no reason for the crown to weaken further in the second half of this year but said its future direction would depend on the government's ability to restore investor confidence and attract long-term capital.
However, some analysts say extra demand for money to finance reconstruction will keep rates at current relatively high levels and this could delay when the crown finds its new post-float equilibrium.
"It will be much more difficult for the central bank to continue lowering interest rates than it would be without the floods," said Krovak.
He said he expected the floods to widen the trade deficit, both through lost exports and extra imports for reconstruction, but to help the capital account through higher interest rates.
"It is too early to say which of these tendencies will prevail," he said.

Expandia Finance chief economist Miroslav Singer said that, assuming one to two weeks of lost production in the affected regions, the floods could cut 1997 industrial output by one percentage point but said the expected fall was already reflected in the crown rate.
He also said it would be harder to enforce a wage freeze.
The CNB said in a statement on July 17 that the floods should not be allowed to lead to a change in monetary policy and that flood relief should not mean a retreat from austerity.
The bank said the government should consider a temporary, exceptional hike in personal income tax.
"Despite the floods, we are still faced with the main problem -- the imbalance of the current account...which must be solved," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters.
"The way to do this is not to allow the state budget to run a deficit but to lower demand in the economy and to base growth in the economy on growing exports," he said.
The bank has indicated it is prepared to intervene with interest rate hikes if it sees a danger of inflation. ($ = 34.47 Czech Crowns)
